    paragraph_summary: 'Dr. Alexander Motyl, a Political Science Professor at Rutgers
      University, assesses the likelihood of a leadership change in Russia, particularly
      regarding Vladimir Putin''s regime. He references Edward Luttwak’s framework from
      "Coup d’Etat: A Practical Handbook" to argue that the current conditions in Russia—characterized
      by restricted political participation, a centralized political structure, and

      that these elements indicate a significant possibility for a transition in leadership,
      urging that Russia should prepare for the implications of such a change.'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/03/u-s-air-force-f-15e-strike-eagle-fighter-was-built-for-a-war-just-like-iran/
    text: The shootdown of three USAF F-15E Strike Eagles by friendly Kuwaiti Air Defense
      on March 2, 2026, stands as the most significant "blue-on-blue" incident of the
      21st century. While all six crew members safely ejected 6.2 miles from Ali Al
      Salem Air Base, the disaster exposes critical friction in the coalition's command-and-control
      (C2) architecture during the height of Operation Epic Fury. The post U.S. Air
      Force F-15E Strike Eagle Fighter Was Built for a War Just Like Iran appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The friendly fire incident involving the shootdown of three
      USAF F-15E Strike Eagles by Kuwaiti Air Defense on March 2, 2026, highlights significant
      flaws in coalition command-and-control systems during Operation Epic Fury, despite
      all crew members safely ejecting.
    paragraph_summary: On March 2, 2026, three USAF F-15E Strike Eagles were mistakenly
      shot down by Kuwaiti Air Defense, marking the most significant "blue-on-blue"
      incident of the 21st century. Fortunately, all six crew members ejected safely
      about 6.2 miles from Ali Al Salem Air Base. This incident highlights serious issues

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/03/10-minutes-of-play-how-staffing-shortages-at-joint-base-san-antonio-lackland-led-to-military-working-dog-deaths/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Stephen Silver, an award-winning national security
      journalist, evaluates the DoD Inspector General’s report on the Military Working
      Dog (MWD) Program. -Authored by Randolph R. Stone, the evaluation found that the
      341st Training Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland failed to provide the
      mandated five hours of daily engagement, leading to heat […] The post 10 Minutes
      of Play: How Staffing Shortages at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland Led to Military
      Working Dog Deaths appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Stephen Silver's evaluation of the DoD Inspector General's
      report reveals that staffing shortages at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland resulted
      in the 341st Training Squadron failing to meet the required daily engagement for
      Military Working Dogs, contributing to their deaths.
    paragraph_summary: In an evaluation of the Department of Defense Inspector General's
      report on the Military Working Dog (MWD) Program, journalist Stephen Silver highlights
      significant shortcomings at the 341st Training Squadron in Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland.
      Authored by Randolph R. Stone, the report reveals that the squadron failed to
      meet the required five hours of daily engagement for the dogs, which contributed
      to tragic incidents, including the deaths of military working dogs due to heat-related
      issues. The findings underscore the impact of staffing shortages on the welfare
      of these animals and raise concerns about the overall management of the MWD Program.

      a viable path to achieving victory in the ongoing conflict.

  - title: 'Red Sword: China’s J-20 Mighty Dragon Stealth Fighter and H-6 Bombers Take
      Part in Massive Secret Air War Simulation'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/03/red-sword-chinas-j-20-mighty-dragon-stealth-fighter-and-h-6-bombers-takes-part-in-massive-secret-air-war-simulation/
    text: 'The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) has quietly executed its largest-ever
      air combat exercise, a massive 200-aircraft operation that signals a radical shift
      from "flashy" posturing to high-end, integrated warfare. According to a February
      25, 2026, briefing at the Air & Space Forces Association Warfare Symposium, this
      Red Sword exercise utilized eight remote air bases in Western China to rehearse
      the kind of complex, multi-generation tactics that the U.S. Air Force pioneered
      with Red Flag. The post Red Sword: China’s J-20 Mighty Dragon Stealth Fighter
      and H-6 Bombers Take Part in Massive Secret Air War Simulation appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The People’s Liberation Army Air Force conducted its largest
      air combat exercise, involving 200 aircraft and advanced tactics, marking a significant
      transition towards integrated warfare capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) has conducted
      its largest air combat exercise to date, involving 200 aircraft in a significant
      shift towards advanced integrated warfare tactics. This operation, named Red Sword,
      took place across eight remote air bases in Western China and was highlighted
      during a briefing at the Air & Space Forces Association Warfare Symposium on February
      25, 2026. The exercise focused on complex, multi-generation tactics similar to
      those developed by the U.S. Air Force in its Red Flag exercises, showcasing China's
      evolving military capabilities with the participation of advanced aircraft like
      the J-20 stealth fighter and H-6 bombers.
    published: '2026-03-02T14:24:59+00:00'

    text: 'The 2015 "sinking" of the USS Theodore Roosevelt by the French Rubis-class

      evidence for a "Carrier Vulnerability" doctrine that now dictates U.S. naval planning
      in the face of quiet, lethal undersea threats. The post ‘Sir, We Have Been Hit’:

    one_sentence_summary: The 2015 incident where the French submarine Saphir "sank"
      the USS Theodore Roosevelt has led to a significant shift in U.S. naval strategy,
      highlighting the vulnerability of aircraft carriers to silent underwater threats
      and shaping current naval planning.
    paragraph_summary: The 2015 incident involving the French Rubis-class submarine
      Saphir "sinking" the USS Theodore Roosevelt has become a pivotal moment in naval
      history, highlighting the vulnerabilities of aircraft carriers to stealthy underwater
      threats. This event is no longer seen as an isolated occurrence but has instead
      shaped a new "Carrier Vulnerability" doctrine that influences U.S. naval strategy
      and planning. The implications of this exercise underscore the need for heightened
      awareness and adaptation in the face of advanced submarine capabilities within
      modern warfare.

  - title: The Javelin Missile Is a Proven Tank Killer Russia Hates in Ukraine. And
      Then the Drones Started Flying
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/03/the-javelin-missile-is-a-proven-tank-killer-russia-hates-in-ukraine-and-then-the-drones-started-flying/
    text: The FGM-148 Javelin, once the "Saint" of the early Ukrainian resistance, has
      moved from a viral sensation to a niche tool in a 2026 battlespace dominated by
      First-Person View (FPV) loitering munitions. While the Javelin remains the "gold
      standard" for man-portable anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs), the brutal math
      of attrition and the $200,000 price tag have forced a shift in tactical priority.
      The post The Javelin Missile Is a Proven Tank Killer Russia Hates in Ukraine.
      And Then the Drones Started Flying appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The FGM-148 Javelin, once a key asset in Ukraine's early resistance
      against Russia, has become less central in a 2026 combat landscape increasingly
      dominated by FPV loitering munitions, despite still being regarded as a top anti-tank
      missile due to its high cost and the realities of attrition warfare.
    paragraph_summary: The FGM-148 Javelin missile, initially celebrated for its effectiveness
      in the early stages of the Ukrainian resistance, has transitioned from a widely
      recognized asset to a more specialized tool in the evolving 2026 battlefield,
      which is now heavily influenced by First-Person View (FPV) loitering munitions.
      Despite being regarded as the "gold standard" for man-portable anti-tank guided
      missiles (ATGMs), the high cost of $200,000 and the realities of attrition warfare
      have necessitated a reevaluation of tactical priorities, diminishing the Javelin's
      prominence as drone technology gains traction in combat scenarios.
    published: '2026-03-02T02:24:16+00:00'

      as a significant example of the shift from traditional 4th-generation dogfighting
      to modern 5th-generation sensor-driven warfare. While the F-35 achieved an impressive

  - title: 'The Problem with the Iran War of 2026: America Doesn’t Know What It Wants'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-problem-with-the-iran-war-of-2026-america-doesnt-know-what-it-wants/
    text: 'The U.S. is "pounding" Iran, but history says you can''t drop a new government
      from a bomb bay. From the failed hunt for Saddam to the "temporary" win in Afghanistan,
      Dr. Robert Farley warns that airpower is great at breaking things, but terrible
      at building them. The post The Problem with the Iran War of 2026: America Doesn’t
      Know What It Wants appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Dr. Robert Farley argues that while the U.S. may effectively
      use airpower to disrupt Iran, historical precedents show that military force alone
      fails to establish stable governments or constructive outcomes.
    paragraph_summary: In the article, Dr. Robert Farley argues that while the U.S.
      may be aggressively targeting Iran with airpower, historical precedents demonstrate
      that military force alone cannot successfully establish a new government or ensure
      stability. He references past failures in Iraq and Afghanistan, highlighting that
      while airstrikes can effectively destroy infrastructure and military capabilities,
      they fall short in nation-building and creating lasting peace. Farley emphasizes
      that the U.S. lacks a clear strategy or understanding of its objectives in the
      potential conflict with Iran, raising concerns about the effectiveness of a purely
      military approach.
    published: '2026-02-28T18:18:43+00:00'

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Dr. Michael Rubin, a former Pentagon official, analyzes

    paragraph_summary: In his analysis, Dr. Michael Rubin, a former Pentagon official,
      examines the historical precedents of using airpower for regime change, specifically

      victory despite airstrikes. Rubin suggests that simply relying on bombing to achieve
      regime change may not be effective, as history indicates the complexities involved
      in such military actions.

  - title: 'Russia’s Su-57 Felon Has a Big Problem: It Might Not Be a Real Stealth Fighter
      Like the F-22 or F-35'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/russias-su-57-felon-has-a-big-problem-it-might-not-be-a-real-stealth-fighter-like-the-f-22-or-f-35/
    text: 'Russia markets the Su-57 as a fifth-generation stealth fighter, but critics
      argue its stealth is overstated. The piece highlights claims that Sukhoi documentation
      places the jet’s frontal radar cross-section around 0.1 to 1 square meters—closer
      to non-stealth aircraft than to the F-35—along with assertions that stealth-driven
      detection gaps explain lopsided training outcomes. The post Russia’s Su-57 Felon
      Has a Big Problem: It Might Not Be a Real Stealth Fighter Like the F-22 or F-35
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Critics argue that Russia's Su-57 stealth fighter may not
      possess true stealth capabilities, as its radar cross-section measurements suggest
      it is more comparable to non-stealth aircraft than to advanced fighters like the
      F-35 and F-22.
    paragraph_summary: The article critiques Russia's Su-57 stealth fighter, suggesting
      that its stealth capabilities may be exaggerated compared to true fifth-generation
      fighters like the F-22 and F-35. It references Sukhoi documentation indicating
      that the Su-57's frontal radar cross-section ranges from 0.1 to 1 square meters,
      which aligns more closely with non-stealth aircraft than its Western counterparts.
      Additionally, the piece discusses how these potential stealth deficiencies could
      contribute to unfavorable training outcomes for the Su-57, raising questions about
      its effectiveness in modern aerial combat.
    published: '2026-02-28T00:08:34+00:00'

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: A Lockheed test mission in 1966 turned into a near-instant

    one_sentence_summary: In a 1966 test mission, an SR-71 Blackbird experienced a catastrophic

    paragraph_summary: In a 1966 test mission, an SR-71 Blackbird experienced a catastrophic
      right-inlet malfunction while flying at Mach 3.18 and 79,000 feet, leading to
      a critical loss of control during a steep bank maneuver. The inlet unstart caused
      violent yaw, roll, and pitch, significantly compromising the aircraft's stability.
      This perilous situation culminated in the disintegration of the aircraft, resulting
      in the pilot being ejected from the cockpit. The incident highlights the extreme
      risks associated with operating at such high speeds and altitudes.

  - title: 'Psychology Suggests the U.S. Army Needs to Do More To Battle A New Enemy
      (Not Russia or China): Loneliness'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/psychology-suggests-the-u-s-army-needs-to-do-more-to-battle-a-new-enemy-not-russia-or-china-loneliness/
    text: 'A Harvard Business Review study published in 2017 argued the U.S. Army knows
      how to build unit cohesion, but needed sharper tools to reduce loneliness and
      strengthen “social resilience.” Researchers tested dozens of “social fitness”
      exercises—ranging from simple favors to structured group problem-solving—and reported
      reduced loneliness and improved well-being. The post Psychology Suggests the U.S.
      Army Needs to Do More To Battle A New Enemy (Not Russia or China): Loneliness
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: A 2017 Harvard Business Review study found that while the
      U.S. Army excels at fostering unit cohesion, it requires more effective strategies
      to combat loneliness and enhance social resilience, demonstrating that various
      "social fitness" exercises can significantly improve well-being among soldiers.
    paragraph_summary: A 2017 study from Harvard Business Review highlighted that while
      the U.S. Army excels at fostering unit cohesion, it requires more effective strategies
      to combat loneliness and enhance "social resilience." Researchers experimented
      with various "social fitness" exercises, including simple acts of kindness and
      organized group problem-solving, which resulted in decreased feelings of loneliness
      and improved overall well-being among soldiers. The findings suggest that addressing
      loneliness is crucial for the Army's mental health initiatives, as it represents
      a significant challenge beyond traditional military threats.
    published: '2026-02-27T15:40:48+00:00'

  - title: The ‘Super’ F-22 Raptor Stealth Fighter Could Be a Nightmare For China
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-super-f-22-raptor-stealth-fighter-could-be-a-nightmare-for-china/
    text: The unveiling of the "F-22 Raptor 2.0" concept at the Air & Space Forces Association’s
      (AFA) 2026 Warfare Symposium represents a critical pivot for Lockheed Martin following
      its loss of the NGAD (F-47) contract to Boeing. The focus has shifted from replacing
      the Raptor to evolving it into a 6th-generation bridge, integrating AI-driven
      electronic warfare and external stealth sensors to counter the proliferation of
      China’s J-20 and J-35 fleets in the Indo-Pacific. The post The ‘Super’ F-22 Raptor
      Stealth Fighter Could Be a Nightmare For China appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Lockheed Martin's introduction of the "F-22 Raptor 2.0" concept
      at the AFA 2026 Warfare Symposium marks a strategic shift to enhance the existing
      Raptor with advanced AI and stealth capabilities, aiming to address challenges
      posed by China's growing military aircraft fleet.
    paragraph_summary: At the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Warfare Symposium,
      Lockheed Martin introduced the "F-22 Raptor 2.0" concept, marking a strategic
      shift after losing the NGAD (F-47) contract to Boeing. Instead of developing a
      new aircraft to replace the Raptor, the company aims to enhance the existing model
      into a 6th-generation fighter, incorporating AI-driven electronic warfare capabilities
      and advanced external stealth sensors. This evolution is designed to address the
      growing threat posed by China's J-20 and J-35 fleets in the Indo-Pacific region.

  - title: The U.S. Air Force Is ‘Missing’ Over 100 B-2 Spirit Stealth Bombers
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-u-s-air-force-is-missing-over-100-b-2-spirit-stealth-bombers/
    text: 'The B-2 Spirit’s role in the "Midnight Hammer" strikes against Fordow last
      summer has solidified its status as America’s only viable "bunker-buster" platform
      until the 2030s. However, Brandon J. Weichert’s analysis highlights a critical
      strategic fragility: with only 19 airworthy bombers remaining, the loss of even
      a single airframe—as seen in the 2022 fire—represents a significant degradation
      of the U.S. nuclear and conventional "Deep Strike" capability. The post The U.S.
      Air Force Is ‘Missing’ Over 100 B-2 Spirit Stealth Bombers appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The B-2 Spirit has proven essential as America's primary "bunker-buster"
      for deep strike missions, but its limited fleet of only 19 operational bombers
      poses a strategic risk, as the loss of any one could severely impact U.S. military
      capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: The B-2 Spirit stealth bomber has solidified its role as America's
      primary "bunker-buster" platform following its involvement in the "Midnight Hammer"
      strikes against Fordow last summer. However, Brandon J. Weichert's analysis reveals
      a concerning strategic vulnerability, as the U.S. Air Force currently has only
      19 operational B-2 bombers. The loss of even one aircraft, as demonstrated by
      a fire incident in 2022, could significantly impair the U.S.'s nuclear and conventional
      "Deep Strike" capabilities, highlighting the urgent need for a more robust fleet.
    published: '2026-02-26T15:49:53+00:00'

  - title: The U.S. Navy Is Missing 26 Seawolf-Class Nuclear Attack Submarines
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-u-s-navy-is-missing-26-seawolf-class-nuclear-attack-submarines/
    text: The decision to cap the Seawolf-class at only three hulls remains one of the
      most debated "peace dividend" trade-offs of the post-Cold War era. As the U.S.
      Navy now faces a massive industrial backlog and a rapidly expanding People’s Liberation
      Army Navy (PLAN), the absence of the 26 "missing" Seawolf submarines has left
      a gap in high-end undersea dominance that the smaller Virginia-class was never
      designed to fill. The post The U.S. Navy Is Missing 26 Seawolf-Class Nuclear Attack
      Submarines appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy's decision to limit the Seawolf-class submarines
      to just three hulls has created a significant gap in undersea capabilities amid
      increasing naval competition with China, as the smaller Virginia-class submarines
      cannot adequately replace the missing 26 Seawolf submarines.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy's decision to limit the Seawolf-class submarines
      to just three hulls is a contentious issue from the post-Cold War period, often
      viewed as a significant "peace dividend" trade-off. Currently, the Navy is grappling
      with a substantial industrial backlog and the growing capabilities of the People's
      Liberation Army Navy (PLAN), which has highlighted the strategic shortfall created
      by the absence of 26 planned Seawolf submarines. The smaller Virginia-class submarines,
      while operational, were not designed to replace the advanced capabilities that
      the Seawolf-class would have provided, leaving a critical gap in the Navy's undersea
      dominance.
    published: '2026-02-26T15:22:40+00:00'

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Brandon J. Weichert, a Senior National Security Editor
      and iHeartRadio host, provides an analysis of the SSN(X) next-generation attack
      submarine program and its critical failures. -Designed to combine Seawolf-class

    one_sentence_summary: Brandon J. Weichert critiques the SSN(X) next-generation attack
      submarine program, highlighting its significant delays and challenges stemming
      from a fragile industrial base, which may push its completion to the 2040s.
    paragraph_summary: Brandon J. Weichert, a Senior National Security Editor, critiques
      the SSN(X) next-generation attack submarine program, highlighting its significant
      shortcomings. Intended to merge the high speed of the Seawolf-class with the stealth
      capabilities of the Virginia-class, the project is now delayed until the 2040s
      due to a fragile industrial base and dry dock issues. Weichert draws parallels
      between the SSN(X) and the troubled F-35 program, suggesting that the submarine
      initiative is facing similar challenges that threaten its viability.

    one_sentence_summary: Isaac Seitz highlights General George S. Patton's strategic

      examines General George S. Patton's tactical acumen during the 1944 Battle of

      plans that enabled a swift response to the unexpected German offensive. This operational
      readiness allowed Patton to execute a rapid 90-degree maneuver toward Bastogne,

      also features a military quote from Patton, emphasizing that success in warfare
      relies more on strategy and leadership than on technological advancements.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/white-emperor-con-job-why-chinas-hypersonic-space-fighter-just-went-silent-in-2026/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Harrison Kass, a JD and former U.S. Air Force pilot
      selectee, deconstructs the Baidi (White Emperor) “space-air fighter” unveiled
      by AVIC at the 2024 Zhuhai Airshow. -While the tailless diamond-wing design promised
      hypersonic speeds and near-space capabilities, its subsequent disappearance from
      the PLAAF development pipeline suggests a “propaganda-first” strategy. -This 19FortyFive
      […] The post White Emperor Con Job: Why China’s Hypersonic “Space Fighter” Just
      Went Silent in 2026 appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Harrison Kass analyzes the Baidi "space-air fighter" revealed
      by AVIC at the 2024 Zhuhai Airshow, highlighting its ambitious design for hypersonic
      speeds and near-space capabilities, but notes its absence from the PLAAF development
      pipeline indicates a focus on propaganda rather than practical military advancement.
    paragraph_summary: Harrison Kass, a JD and former U.S. Air Force pilot selectee,
      analyzes the Baidi (White Emperor) "space-air fighter" introduced by AVIC at the
      2024 Zhuhai Airshow, highlighting its tailless diamond-wing design that claimed
      to achieve hypersonic speeds and near-space capabilities. However, the fighter's
      subsequent removal from the People's Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) development
      pipeline indicates that it may have been more of a propaganda effort than a viable
      military project. Kass suggests that the fighter's silence in 2026 reflects a
      broader trend in China's defense strategy focused on showcasing advanced technology
      rather than delivering operational capabilities.

      as an Interim Final Rule on February 17, 2026, the regulation sought to counter

    one_sentence_summary: Stephen Silver reports that the Department of Veterans Affairs
      has no intentions of addressing the controversial disability rating rule established
      in response to the Ingram v. Collins court decision, following significant backlash.
    paragraph_summary: 'Stephen Silver, a national security journalist, discusses the
      Department of Veterans Affairs'' (VA) swift withdrawal from its proposed regulation,
      the "Evaluative Rating: Impact of Medication," which was intended to address the
      Ingram v. Collins court ruling regarding disability ratings. Published as an Interim
      Final Rule on February 17, 2026, the regulation aimed to modify how disabilities
      are assessed, but the VA has now indicated that it has no plans to take any further
      action on this issue, raising concerns about the future of disability evaluations
      for veterans.'

      to Survive S-400 Zones'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/stealth-gap-why-the-eurofighter-typhoon-requires-f-35-stealth-protection-to-survive-s-400-zones/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Harrison Kass, a JD and former U.S. Air Force pilot
      selectee, breaks down the strategic evolution of the Eurofighter Typhoon. Designed
      in the Cold War to intercept MiG-29 and Su-27 formations, the Typhoon now bridges
      the gap between 4th and 5th-generation warfare. -Integrating the CAPTOR-E AESA
      radar and the ramjet-powered Meteor […] The post Stealth Gap: Why the Eurofighter
      Typhoon Requires F-35 Stealth Protection to Survive S-400 Zones appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Harrison Kass discusses how the Eurofighter Typhoon, originally
      designed during the Cold War, has evolved to meet modern warfare demands by integrating
      advanced technologies, yet still requires F-35 stealth capabilities to effectively
      operate in areas protected by S-400 missile systems.
    paragraph_summary: Harrison Kass, a JD and former U.S. Air Force pilot selectee,
      analyzes the strategic evolution of the Eurofighter Typhoon, originally designed
      during the Cold War to counter MiG-29 and Su-27 aircraft. He highlights how the
      Typhoon has adapted to bridge the capabilities between 4th and 5th-generation
      warfare, particularly through the integration of advanced technologies like the
      CAPTOR-E AESA radar and the ramjet-powered Meteor missile. Kass argues that despite
      these advancements, the Typhoon still requires the stealth protection of the F-35
      to effectively operate in areas defended by advanced systems like the S-400.

      highlights the often-overlooked close-quarters combat capabilities of the Grumman

      wing design significantly enhanced its performance in Basic Fighter Maneuvers

      between the pilot's skills and the aircraft's unique features, Seitz argues that
      the F-14 was effectively a "knife fighter" in disguise, capable of engaging in
      close-range combat despite its primary role.

      Raptor and the German Luftwaffe’s Eurofighter Typhoon. -While the Raptor remains
      the premier 5th-generation stealth fighter, this analysis explores how Basic Fighter
      Maneuvers (BFM) and within-visual-range (WVR) constraints neutralized the […]

    one_sentence_summary: Isaac Seitz analyzes the 2012 Red Flag Alaska engagement,
      highlighting how Basic Fighter Maneuvers and within-visual-range constraints allowed
      a German Eurofighter Typhoon to effectively neutralize the U.S. Air Force's F-22
      Raptor, despite its status as a premier stealth fighter.
    paragraph_summary: In his analysis of the 2012 Red Flag Alaska engagement, defense
      columnist Isaac Seitz examines the confrontation between the U.S. Air Force's
      F-22 Raptor and Germany's Eurofighter Typhoon, highlighting how Basic Fighter
      Maneuvers (BFM) and within-visual-range (WVR) tactics diminished the Raptor's
      advantages as a premier 5th-generation stealth fighter. Despite the F-22's advanced
      capabilities, the engagement showcased vulnerabilities that allowed the Eurofighter
      to effectively "shoot down" the Raptor, prompting a reevaluation of air combat
      strategies and the effectiveness of stealth technology in close-range dogfights.

  - title: 'Monday Life Inspiration Quote of the Day by ‘Winston Churchill’: ‘Optimism
      is going after Moby Dick in a rowboat and taking tartar sauce with you..’'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/monday-life-inspiration-quote-of-the-day-by-winston-churchill-optimism-is-going-after-moby-dick-in-a-rowboat-and-taking-tartar-sauce-with-you/
    text: 'Winston Churchill is the ultimate symbol of British resilience, yet his 2026
      legacy is increasingly defined by the "rowboat optimism" that led to some of his
      greatest 1920s disasters. While the world remembers him for the "V for Victory"
      sign of the 1940s, the decade preceding his "wilderness years" was marked by economic
      blunders, brutal parliamentary forces in Ireland, and a failed crusade against
      the Bolsheviks. The post Monday Life Inspiration Quote of the Day by ‘Winston
      Churchill’: ‘Optimism is going after Moby Dick in a rowboat and taking tartar
      sauce with you..’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Winston Churchill, often seen as a symbol of British resilience,
      is increasingly remembered for the misguided "rowboat optimism" that characterized
      his economic and political failures in the 1920s, overshadowing his later iconic
      status during World War II.
    paragraph_summary: 'Winston Churchill, often celebrated as a symbol of British resilience,
      is increasingly remembered for the "rowboat optimism" that characterized his approach
      during the 1920s, leading to significant failures such as economic missteps, conflicts
      in Ireland, and a failed campaign against the Bolsheviks. While his "V for Victory"
      sign from the 1940s remains iconic, the decade before his "wilderness years" was
      fraught with challenges that overshadow his later successes. A quote attributed
      to him humorously encapsulates this mindset: “Optimism is going after Moby Dick
      in a rowboat and taking tartar sauce with you.”'
    published: '2026-02-23T19:04:16+00:00'

      in its role within the U.S. Navy.

  - title: 'Sweden ‘Sank’ a U.S. Navy Aircraft Carrier: How One Wargame Showed How America’s
      Supercarriers Can Be Beaten'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/sweden-sank-a-u-s-navy-aircraft-carrier-how-one-wargame-showed-how-americas-supercarriers-can-be-beaten/
    text: 'The 2005 wargames involving the HSwMS Gotland and the USS Ronald Reagan remain
      a watershed moment in naval history. While the multi-billion dollar nuclear carrier
      was protected by a fortress of destroyers and subs, the $100 million Swedish diesel
      boat proved that in the "quiet spaces" of the ocean, a "David" can indeed topple
      a "Goliath." This exercise is still the primary case study for the "asymmetric
      cost curve" in modern maritime warfare. The post Sweden ‘Sank’ a U.S. Navy Aircraft
      Carrier: How One Wargame Showed How America’s Supercarriers Can Be Beaten appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The 2005 wargames demonstrated that a smaller, less expensive
      submarine like the HSwMS Gotland can effectively challenge and potentially defeat
      a heavily protected nuclear aircraft carrier, highlighting the concept of asymmetric
      warfare in naval strategy.
    paragraph_summary: The 2005 wargames featuring the HSwMS Gotland and the USS Ronald
      Reagan marked a significant event in naval history, demonstrating that a relatively
      inexpensive Swedish diesel submarine could successfully challenge the heavily
      protected, multi-billion dollar U.S. nuclear carrier. This exercise highlighted
      the concept of the "asymmetric cost curve" in modern maritime warfare, illustrating
      how smaller, less costly forces can effectively counter larger, more expensive
      ones. The scenario remains a key case study in understanding the vulnerabilities
      of supercarriers in naval operations.
    published: '2026-02-23T15:51:17+00:00'

    text: 'The USS Missouri (BB-63) remains one of the most storied vessels in American

      by its role in the Japanese surrender of WWII. The legacy of the "Mighty Mo" is

      the role of the battleship in the jet age—transforming from a ship-killer into
      a massive, floating artillery battery that sustained the UN front during its darkest
      hours. The post Sailed Right Into a Hurricane: Iowa-Class Battleship USS Missouri
      Did the Unthinkable to Attack North Korea appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The USS Missouri, renowned for its role in WWII, played a
      pivotal yet often overlooked part in the Korean War by evolving from a traditional
      battleship into a crucial artillery support platform for UN forces.
    paragraph_summary: The USS Missouri (BB-63), renowned for its historical significance
      in American naval history, particularly during World War II, also played a crucial
      role in the Korean War (1950–1953), a period often overshadowed by its earlier
      achievements. Known as the "Mighty Mo," this battleship evolved from a traditional
      ship-killer into a formidable floating artillery platform that provided vital
      support to UN forces during challenging times. Its legacy extends beyond its status
      as a museum in Pearl Harbor, highlighting its transformative impact on naval warfare
      in the jet age.

  - title: The U.S. Air Force’s B-52 Bomber Could Once Again Be Ready to Drop Nuclear
      Bombs
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-u-s-air-forces-b-52-bomber-could-once-again-be-ready-to-drop-nuclear-bombs/
    text: The B-52 Stratofortress, the venerable "BUFF," is preparing for a return to
      its original Cold War roots. Following the expiration of the New START treaty
      without a successor, Air Force Global Strike Command (AFGSC) has signaled its
      readiness to restore nuclear capabilities to the entire 76-ship fleet. This shift,
      combined with a massive modernization effort, ensures that an airframe designed
      in the 1950s will remain a cornerstone of the U.S. nuclear triad for the next
      quarter-century. The post The U.S. Air Force’s B-52 Bomber Could Once Again Be
      Ready to Drop Nuclear Bombs appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The B-52 Stratofortress is set to revive its Cold War-era
      nuclear capabilities as the U.S. Air Force prepares to modernize the fleet in
      response to the expiration of the New START treaty.
    paragraph_summary: The B-52 Stratofortress, also known as the "BUFF," is set to
      revert to its Cold War-era nuclear capabilities as the Air Force Global Strike
      Command (AFGSC) prepares to enhance the entire fleet of 76 bombers following the
      lapse of the New START treaty. This strategic shift, coupled with a significant
      modernization initiative, ensures that the B-52, originally designed in the 1950s,
      will continue to play a vital role in the U.S. nuclear triad for at least the
      next 25 years.

  - title: The SR-72 Could Hit Mach 6 But Keeps Missing Deadlines and May Never Fly
      Anywhere
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-sr-72-could-hit-mach-6-but-keeps-missing-deadlines-and-may-never-fly-anywhere/
    text: The SR-72 "Son of Blackbird" is the most elusive titan of the 2026 aerospace
      landscape. While its 2025 "first flight" deadline passed without a public sonic
      boom, the trail of billion-dollar financial losses and classified facility expansions
      at Lockheed Martin suggests that the Mach 6 successor to the SR-71 is far from
      a ghost. It is likely the first aircraft to bridge the "valley of death" between
      traditional turbines and hypersonic scramjets. The post The SR-72 Could Hit Mach
      6 But Keeps Missing Deadlines and May Never Fly Anywhere appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .
    one_sentence_summary: The SR-72, a hypersonic aircraft intended to surpass the SR-71,
      remains shrouded in secrecy and has missed its 2025 flight deadline, yet significant
      investments and developments at Lockheed Martin indicate it is still a viable
      project aimed at achieving Mach 6 speeds.
    paragraph_summary: The SR-72, known as the "Son of Blackbird," is a highly anticipated
      hypersonic aircraft that aims to reach speeds of Mach 6, yet it has missed its
      2025 first flight deadline without any public demonstration. Despite the absence
      of a sonic boom, significant financial investments and expansions at Lockheed
      Martin indicate that the project is still active and not merely a phantom. The
      SR-72 is expected to be the first aircraft capable of transitioning between traditional
      turbine engines and hypersonic scramjets, although its future remains uncertain
      as it continues to face delays.

  - title: '‘Time Traveling’ with the U.S. Air Force: SR-71 Blackbird Flew So Fast It
      Landed at Beale AFB Almost Day Before Leaving From Kadena AB'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/time-traveling-with-the-u-s-air-force-sr-71-blackbird-flew-so-fast-it-landed-at-beale-afb-almost-day-before-leaving-from-kadena-ab/
    text: 'The SR-71 Blackbird is more than just a piece of Cold War aviation history;
      it remains a masterclass in engineering that, in 2026, still holds the title of
      the fastest crewed, air-breathing aircraft ever put into service. While modern
      hypersonic programs often struggle with thermal management, the Blackbird was
      solving these physics puzzles in the 1960s, famously flying so fast that it could
      literally "race the sun" and land in California nearly a day before it departed
      from Japan. The post ‘Time Traveling’ with the U.S. Air Force: SR-71 Blackbird
      Flew So Fast It Landed at Beale AFB Almost Day Before Leaving From Kadena AB appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The SR-71 Blackbird, an engineering marvel from the Cold War
      era, remains the fastest crewed, air-breathing aircraft as of 2026, having mastered
      thermal management challenges long before modern hypersonic programs.
    paragraph_summary: The SR-71 Blackbird, a remarkable feat of Cold War engineering,
      continues to hold the record as the fastest crewed, air-breathing aircraft as
      of 2026. This iconic aircraft, which could "race the sun" and land in California
      almost a day before its departure from Japan, showcased advanced solutions to
      thermal management challenges that modern hypersonic programs still grapple with
      today. Its legacy as a pioneering technological achievement in aviation remains
      significant.

  - title: 'Stealth Boondoggle: Why the U.S. Navy’s F/A-XX Fighter Fantasy Broke the
      Pentagon'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/stealth-boondoggle-why-the-u-s-navys-f-a-xx-fighter-fantasy-broke-the-pentagon/
    text: 'The 2026 defense landscape is defined by a brutal tug-of-war between legacy
      carrier-based ambitions and the "all-in" prioritization of the Boeing F-47. While
      the Navy views the F/A-XX as a prerequisite for the carrier’s continued relevance,
      the Trump Administration has made it clear that the U.S. defense industrial base—already
      cracking under the strain of 1980s-era procurement models—cannot sustain two simultaneous
      "boutique" air superiority programs. The post Stealth Boondoggle: Why the U.S.
      Navy’s F/A-XX Fighter Fantasy Broke the Pentagon appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The 2026 defense landscape is characterized by a conflict
      between the Navy's need for the F/A-XX fighter to maintain carrier relevance and
      the Trump Administration's focus on the Boeing F-47, amid concerns that the defense
      industrial base cannot support two competing air superiority programs.
    paragraph_summary: The 2026 defense landscape is characterized by a conflict between
      the U.S. Navy's desire to advance carrier-based capabilities through the F/A-XX
      program and the Trump Administration's commitment to prioritizing the Boeing F-47,
      which poses challenges for the already strained defense industrial base. The Navy
      believes the F/A-XX is essential for maintaining the relevance of aircraft carriers,
      but the administration has indicated that it cannot support two competing air
      superiority programs simultaneously, reflecting concerns over outdated procurement
      models from the 1980s.
    published: '2026-02-23T13:31:32+00:00'

  - title: '‘B-2 Bomber’ Flying from Aircraft Carrier: A-12 Avenger II Stealth Bomber
      Has A Message for the U.S. Navy'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/b-2-bomber-flying-from-aircraft-carrier-a-12-avenger-ii-stealth-bomber-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-navy/
    text: 'The A-12 Avenger II, famously dubbed the "Flying Dorito," remains one of
      the most expensive and ambitious failures in the history of naval aviation. Intended
      to be the U.S. Navy’s premier stealthy carrier-based strike bomber, the program
      was terminated in 1991 by then-Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney. In 2026, as the
      Navy faces new challenges with the F/A-XX and NGAD programs, the A-12 stands as
      a cautionary tale about the dangers of "PowerPoint realism" and the "unrealistic
      assumptions" of the defense industrial base. The post ‘B-2 Bomber’ Flying from
      Aircraft Carrier: A-12 Avenger II Stealth Bomber Has A Message for the U.S. Navy
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The A-12 Avenger II, an ambitious but ultimately failed stealth
      bomber program terminated in 1991, serves as a cautionary tale for the U.S. Navy
      regarding the pitfalls of unrealistic expectations in defense projects as it navigates
      new challenges with current programs.
    paragraph_summary: The A-12 Avenger II, known as the "Flying Dorito," is recognized
      as one of the most costly and ambitious failures in naval aviation history, intended
      to serve as the U.S. Navy's leading stealth carrier-based strike bomber before
      its cancellation in 1991 by Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney. As the Navy confronts
      new challenges with the F/A-XX and NGAD programs in 2026, the A-12 serves as a
      cautionary example of the pitfalls of "PowerPoint realism" and the unrealistic
      assumptions prevalent in the defense industrial sector.

  - title: Putin Has a ‘Pathological Fixation’ With NATO
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/putin-has-a-pathological-fixation-with-nato/
    text: 'The "fanatic" label has arguably never been more applicable than to Vladimir
      Putin in 2026. As the Russian President continues his high-intensity campaign
      in Ukraine, his core justification—the "existential threat" of NATO expansion—is
      being increasingly dismissed not just in Europe, but across the Asia-Pacific.
      While the Kremlin continues to frame Russia as a "besieged fortress," the international
      consensus is shifting toward a blunt reality: NATO is the excuse, but the preservation
      of a failing dictatorship is the reason. The post Putin Has a ‘Pathological Fixation’
      With NATO appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: In 2026, Vladimir Putin's justification for his aggressive
      campaign in Ukraine—framing NATO expansion as an "existential threat"—is increasingly
      seen as a facade for preserving his failing dictatorship, as the international
      consensus shifts against his narrative.
    paragraph_summary: 'In 2026, Vladimir Putin''s characterization as a "fanatic" is
      underscored by his ongoing aggressive campaign in Ukraine, where his primary rationale—the
      "existential threat" posed by NATO expansion—is losing credibility not only in
      Europe but also in the Asia-Pacific region. While the Kremlin portrays Russia
      as a "besieged fortress," the global perspective is increasingly recognizing that
      NATO serves merely as a pretext for Putin''s true aim: the maintenance of a failing
      dictatorship.'
    published: '2026-02-22T15:45:14+00:00'

  - title: 'Psychology Suggests ‘Crew Fatigue’ Is Setting In: U.S. Navy Aircraft Carrier
      USS Gerald R. Ford Is Being Pushed Past Any Normal Limits'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/psychology-suggests-crew-fatigue-is-setting-in-u-s-navy-aircraft-carrier-uss-gerald-r-ford-is-being-pushed-past-any-normal-limits/
    text: 'The USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78) is no stranger to the spotlight, but that
      spotlight has turned into a high-intensity interrogation of U.S. naval endurance.
      After a grueling 230-day deployment that saw the capture of Nicolas Maduro in
      Venezuela, the $13 billion "nuclear-powered leviathan" is being "double-pumped"
      back to the Middle East. While its technology is world-class, the structural and
      human costs of this mission are reaching a critical mass. The post Psychology
      Suggests ‘Crew Fatigue’ Is Setting In: U.S. Navy Aircraft Carrier USS Gerald R.
      Ford Is Being Pushed Past Any Normal Limits appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The USS Gerald R. Ford, after a demanding 230-day deployment,
      is being rapidly redeployed to the Middle East, raising concerns about crew fatigue
      and the sustainability of U.S. naval operations despite its advanced technology.
    paragraph_summary: The USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78), a $13 billion nuclear-powered
      aircraft carrier, is facing intense scrutiny following a demanding 230-day deployment
      that included the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro. Now, it is being
      rapidly redeployed to the Middle East, raising concerns about the structural integrity
      of the ship and the well-being of its crew. Experts suggest that "crew fatigue"
      is becoming a significant issue as the vessel is pushed beyond typical operational
      limits, highlighting the challenges of maintaining endurance in U.S. naval operations.
    published: '2026-02-22T15:22:08+00:00'

  - title: '‘Safety Issues Abounded’: The Sad Reasons the F-14 Tomcat Fighter The U.S.
      Navy Loved Had To Be Retired'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/safety-issues-abounded-the-sad-reasons-the-f-14-tomcat-fighter-the-u-s-navy-loved-had-to-be-retired/
    text: 'The F-14 Tomcat remains the ultimate symbol of naval air power, yet its 2006
      retirement left a "speed gap" that the U.S. Navy is still feeling today. While
      the F-15 Eagle evolved into the high-tech F-15EX Eagle II, the Tomcat was grounded
      not by enemy fire, but by the staggering cost of its own maintenance. As the Navy
      prepares to retire the F/A-18 Super Hornet, many are looking back at the "Super
      Tomcat" that might have been. The post ‘Safety Issues Abounded’: The Sad Reasons
      the F-14 Tomcat Fighter The U.S. Navy Loved Had To Be Retired appeared first on
      19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The retirement of the F-14 Tomcat in 2006 due to high maintenance
      costs has created a "speed gap" in U.S. naval air power that is still felt today,
      as the Navy looks back at the potential of a "Super Tomcat" while preparing to
      retire the F/A-18 Super Hornet.
    paragraph_summary: The F-14 Tomcat, a symbol of naval air power, was retired in
      2006 due to high maintenance costs, creating a "speed gap" that the U.S. Navy
      continues to experience. While the F-15 Eagle has been upgraded to the advanced
      F-15EX Eagle II, the Tomcat's retirement was not due to combat losses but rather
      financial constraints. As the Navy prepares to phase out the F/A-18 Super Hornet,
      there is nostalgia for the potential of a "Super Tomcat" that could have been
      developed.
    published: '2026-02-22T14:28:39+00:00'

      inter-hemispheric pivot, transiting from combat operations off the coast of Venezuela

      deployment, transitioning from operations near Venezuela to the Middle East, which

      inter-hemispheric transition from combat off Venezuela to a forward-strike position
      in the Middle East. This extended deployment, reminiscent of Vietnam-era missions,
      is pushing the boundaries of the carrier's nuclear-powered technology and raising

      due to the prolonged operational demands.

  - title: '‘Loud as a Disco’: Russia’s Titanium K-222 Was the Fastest Nuclear Submarine
      Ever But Would Never Survive in Combat with the U.S. Navy'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/loud-as-a-disco-russias-titanium-k-222-was-the-fastest-nuclear-submarine-ever-but-would-never-survive-in-combat-with-the-u-s-navy/
    text: 'The Soviet K-222 (Papa-class) remains a legendary anomaly in naval history:
      the fastest nuclear submarine ever built. While modern 2026 submarine doctrine
      prioritizes near-silent "acoustic invisibility," the K-222 was a titanium-hulled
      speed demon that favored raw velocity over stealth. It achieved a record-breaking
      44.7 knots, but paid a heavy price in noise, cost, and structural stability. The
      post ‘Loud as a Disco’: Russia’s Titanium K-222 Was the Fastest Nuclear Submarine
      Ever But Would Never Survive in Combat with the U.S. Navy appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Soviet K-222, a titanium-hulled nuclear submarine, is
      renowned for being the fastest ever built at 44.7 knots, but its emphasis on speed
      over stealth and structural stability would render it ineffective in combat against
      the U.S. Navy.
    paragraph_summary: The Soviet K-222, known as the Papa-class, is recognized as the
      fastest nuclear submarine ever constructed, achieving a remarkable speed of 44.7
      knots. Unlike contemporary submarine designs that emphasize stealth and "acoustic
      invisibility," the K-222 prioritized speed, resulting in significant drawbacks
      such as high noise levels, increased costs, and potential structural instability.
      Its design and performance would likely render it vulnerable in combat scenarios
      against the U.S. Navy, highlighting the trade-offs between speed and stealth in
      naval warfare.
    published: '2026-02-22T12:40:41+00:00'

  - title: '‘Significant Mechanical Degradation’: The U.S. Navy Just Lost Another Nuclear
      Supercarrier'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/significant-mechanical-degradation-the-u-s-navy-just-lost-another-nuclear-supercarrier/
    text: 'The USS John C. Stennis (CVN-74) is currently the focus of a high-stakes
      race against time at Newport News Shipbuilding. As of February 22, 2026, the carrier
      remains sidelined by a Refueling and Complex Overhaul (RCOH) that is now 14 months
      behind schedule. With the USS Gerald R. Ford pushed to its breaking point in the
      Middle East, the Stennis''s return this October is critical to solving the Navy''s
      "carrier math" crisis. The post ‘Significant Mechanical Degradation’: The U.S.
      Navy Just Lost Another Nuclear Supercarrier appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The USS John C. Stennis is facing a critical delay in its
      Refueling and Complex Overhaul, now 14 months behind schedule, which is essential
      for alleviating the U.S. Navy's carrier shortage as the USS Gerald R. Ford is
      heavily utilized in the Middle East.
    paragraph_summary: The USS John C. Stennis (CVN-74) is currently undergoing a Refueling
      and Complex Overhaul (RCOH) at Newport News Shipbuilding, but as of February 22,
      2026, it is 14 months behind schedule. Its timely return in October is crucial
      for addressing the U.S. Navy's "carrier math" crisis, especially as the USS Gerald
      R. Ford is heavily utilized in the Middle East. The situation highlights the urgency
      of the Stennis's overhaul amidst growing operational demands on the Navy's fleet.

      an extraordinary experience involving a flight from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa

    one_sentence_summary: The Seawolf-class submarines, designed to be the most advanced

      miscalculation by the U.S. Navy.
    paragraph_summary: The Seawolf-class submarines were designed to be the most advanced
      attack submarines in history, with an initial plan for a fleet of 29 to succeed
      the Los Angeles-class. However, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Congress
      drastically reduced the order to only three submarines due to the high cost of
      $3.5 billion per unit. This decision has led to ongoing criticism regarding the
      U.S. Navy's strategic planning and the implications of having a limited number
      of these sophisticated vessels.

      of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose tariffs exceeds
      his constitutional authority, restoring Congress's power over fiscal decisions
      and undermining the administration's ability to leverage tariffs in international
      economic negotiations.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Supreme Court has determined that President Trump's
      application of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose
      tariffs exceeds his constitutional authority, effectively restoring Congress's
      control over fiscal matters. This ruling eliminates the administration's ability
      to leverage flexible tariff threats that were crucial in negotiating significant
      economic agreements with other nations. In light of this decision, President Trump
      has responded defiantly, marking a significant shift in the executive's power
      regarding trade and tariffs.

    paragraph_summary: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, renowned as the fastest air-breathing
      aircraft, achieved remarkable speeds over Mach 3.2 at altitudes of 85,000 feet,

      Air Base to California. With its titanium construction, the SR-71 was never shot

      account highlights the extraordinary capability of the aircraft, noting that it
      could land at Beale Air Force Base almost a full day before its departure from
      Kadena.

      in U.S. armored warfare strategy, as the M60A4 was poised to be a powerful addition
      to the Army's fleet.

  - title: A New VA Rule Might Drop Veterans’ Disability Rating if Medication Improves
      Their Symptoms
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/a-new-va-rule-might-drop-veterans-disability-rating-if-medication-improves-their-symptoms/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Effective February 17, 2026, the VA’s interim final
      rule, “Evaluative Rating: Impact of Medication,” directs examiners to evaluate
      disabilities based on “actual functional impairment” under treatment. -This effectively
      overrides court precedents like Jones v. Shinseki and Ingram v. Collins, which
      previously protected veterans from rating reductions due to medication effectiveness.
      -Major […] The post A New VA Rule Might Drop Veterans’ Disability Rating if Medication
      Improves Their Symptoms appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Starting February 17, 2026, a new VA rule will allow examiners
      to reduce veterans' disability ratings based on improvements in functional impairment
      due to medication, overriding previous court protections.
    paragraph_summary: 'Starting February 17, 2026, the VA''s interim final rule titled
      "Evaluative Rating: Impact of Medication" will require examiners to assess disabilities
      based on the actual functional impairment experienced by veterans while undergoing
      treatment. This new rule supersedes previous court rulings, such as Jones v. Shinseki
      and Ingram v. Collins, which had safeguarded veterans from reductions in their
      disability ratings due to improvements in symptoms from medication. The change
      raises concerns that veterans may face lower disability ratings if their medication
      effectively alleviates their conditions.'
    published: '2026-02-19T16:13:01+00:00'

      importance in regional defense.

  - title: The F-117 Nighthawk Stealth Fighter Has a Message for the F-22 Raptor and
      the U.S. Air Force
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-f-117-nighthawk-stealth-fighter-has-a-message-for-the-f-22-raptor-and-the-u-s-air-force/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: The Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk, developed in total
      secrecy by Skunk Works, was the world’s first operational stealth aircraft. -Its
      radical, faceted design prioritized low observability over aerodynamics, requiring
      fly-by-wire systems to remain stable. -A defining 1982 incident at Area 51—where
      test pilot Tom Morgenfeld safely landed a developmental jet without its […] The
      post The F-117 Nighthawk Stealth Fighter Has a Message for the F-22 Raptor and
      the U.S. Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk, the first operational stealth
      aircraft, showcased a unique design focused on low observability and stability
      through advanced fly-by-wire systems, and its development history offers valuable
      lessons for the F-22 Raptor and the U.S. Air Force.
    paragraph_summary: The Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk, created in secrecy by Skunk Works,
      was the first operational stealth aircraft, featuring a unique faceted design
      that emphasized low observability at the expense of traditional aerodynamics,
      necessitating advanced fly-by-wire systems for stability. A pivotal moment in
      its development occurred in 1982 at Area 51, when test pilot Tom Morgenfeld successfully
      landed a prototype without its landing gear. The article suggests that the lessons
      learned from the F-117's design and operational strategies hold important implications
      for the F-22 Raptor and the U.S. Air Force's future approaches to stealth technology
      and aerial combat.
    published: '2026-02-19T14:29:21+00:00'

      A-12's legacy holds important lessons for the U.S. Navy moving forward.

  - title: 'Warship Destroyed: Why the U.S. Navy Sinks Its Own ‘Battleships’ as Warning
      to Russia and China'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/warship-destroyed-why-the-u-s-navy-sinks-its-own-battleships-as-warning-to-russia-and-china/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: The U.S. Navy’s SINKEX events use decommissioned
      ships as live-fire targets so crews can practice real-world maritime strike and
      gather hard data on how hulls fail under weapons impact. -During Valiant Shield
      24, the ex-USS Cleveland (LPD-7) was towed into position in the North Pacific
      and sunk after extensive environmental cleanup, […] The post Warship Destroyed:
      Why the U.S. Navy Sinks Its Own ‘Battleships’ as Warning to Russia and China appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy conducts SINKEX events, using decommissioned
      ships like the ex-USS Cleveland as live-fire targets during exercises such as
      Valiant Shield 24, to train crews and gather data on hull damage, while also sending
      a strategic message to Russia and China.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy conducts SINKEX events, where decommissioned ships
      are used as live-fire targets for training purposes and to collect data on hull
      integrity under weapon impacts. During the recent Valiant Shield 24 exercise,
      the ex-USS Cleveland (LPD-7) was intentionally sunk in the North Pacific following
      thorough environmental cleanup efforts. These exercises serve not only to enhance
      naval strike capabilities but also send a strategic message to potential adversaries
      like Russia and China regarding the U.S. Navy's operational readiness and commitment
      to maritime security.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/china-doesnt-need-to-sink-navy-aircraft-carriers-to-defeat-them/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: In the 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis, U.S. carrier
      groups exposed a painful Chinese reality: Beijing could not reliably find, track,
      or threaten American flattops operating near Taiwan. -That lesson hardened into
      a blueprint. China prioritized persistent surveillance, long-range maritime strike,
      and an integrated reconnaissance-to-fire architecture built to hold carriers at
      risk […] The post China Doesn’t Need to Sink Navy Aircraft Carriers to Defeat
      Them appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis revealed China's inability
      to effectively track U.S. aircraft carriers, prompting Beijing to develop a strategy
      focused on persistent surveillance and long-range strikes to counteract American
      naval power without necessarily sinking the carriers.
    paragraph_summary: The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis revealed to China its inability
      to effectively locate and threaten U.S. aircraft carriers operating near Taiwan,
      prompting a strategic shift in Beijing's military approach. In response, China
      focused on developing persistent surveillance capabilities, long-range maritime
      strike options, and an integrated reconnaissance-to-fire system designed to pose
      a significant threat to these carriers without necessarily sinking them. This
      new strategy emphasizes the ability to deter and neutralize carrier operations
      through advanced military technology and tactics.
    published: '2026-02-18T14:26:56+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-u-s-navy-cant-build-a-navy-anymore/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Post–Cold War U.S. Navy cuts set the stage, but today’s

      before design maturity, and integrating immature technologies and software at
      scale. -Constellation-class frigates gained about 759 metric tons (roughly 13
      percent) and slid to a 2029 first delivery as U.S.-unique changes […] The post
      The U.S. Navy Can’t Build a Navy Anymore appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses how post-Cold War cuts to the U.S. Navy,
      combined with unstable requirements and premature construction practices, have
      led to significant delays and challenges in building modern naval vessels like
      the Constellation-class frigates.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the challenges faced by the U.S. Navy in
      building new ships, particularly the Constellation-class frigates, which have
      experienced significant delays and weight increases due to unstable requirements,
      premature construction, and the integration of immature technologies. These issues,
      rooted in post-Cold War budget cuts, have led to a projected first delivery date
      of 2029 for the frigates, highlighting a broader pattern of difficulties in naval
      shipbuilding that raises concerns about the Navy's capacity to effectively modernize
      and expand its fleet.
    published: '2026-02-17T23:41:22+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/the-u-s-navy-cant-ever-build-new-stealth-seawolf-class-submarines/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Why the U.S. Navy Built Only 3 Seawolf-class Submarines
      -The Seawolf-class was built to be the Navy’s next leap in undersea dominance:
      stronger HY-100 steel, extreme depth capability, a larger weapons load, and a
      design focused on hunting the most dangerous Soviet submarines. -The original
      plan envisioned a large fleet, but […] The post The U.S. Navy Can’t Ever Build
      New Stealth Seawolf-Class Submarines appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy constructed only three Seawolf-class submarines,
      originally intended for a larger fleet, due to changing strategic priorities and
      budget constraints despite their advanced capabilities designed for undersea dominance
      against Soviet threats.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy's Seawolf-class submarines were designed for superior
      undersea warfare capabilities, featuring advanced materials like HY-100 steel,
      enhanced depth capabilities, and increased weaponry, primarily aimed at countering
      Soviet submarine threats. Despite initial plans for a larger fleet, only three
      submarines were ultimately constructed due to shifting defense priorities, budget
      constraints, and the end of the Cold War, which diminished the perceived need
      for such a robust fleet. As a result, the Navy is unlikely to build new stealth
      Seawolf-class submarines in the future.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/a-war-against-iran-could-open-up-a-pandoras-box-that-wont-be-easy-to-close/
    text: 'War on Iran Would Solve the Wrong Problem: Summary and Key Points  -A major
      U.S. strike campaign could severely damage Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, missile
      networks, and IRGC command nodes. -The deeper issue is what comes after. Physical
      destruction would likely buy time, not resolution, while strengthening Tehran’s
      incentive to sprint toward an overt nuclear deterrent. […] The post A War Against
      Iran Could Open Up a Pandora’s Box That Won’t Be Easy To Close appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: A military strike against Iran may temporarily damage its
      nuclear and military capabilities, but it would likely exacerbate tensions and
      incentivize Tehran to pursue a nuclear deterrent more aggressively, ultimately
      leading to a more complex and unresolved situation.
    paragraph_summary: The article argues that a major U.S. military strike against
      Iran could inflict significant damage on its nuclear facilities, missile systems,
      and military command structures. However, it emphasizes that such an action would
      not address the underlying issues and could ultimately exacerbate tensions. Instead
      of resolving the threat, a military campaign might only delay Iran's nuclear ambitions
      while incentivizing the country to pursue a more overt nuclear deterrent. The
      piece warns that engaging in war with Iran could lead to unpredictable and long-lasting
      consequences, likening it to opening a "Pandora's box."

      by fighting battles; wars are won by choosing…”'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/military-quote-of-the-day-from-general-george-patton-wars-are-not-won-by-fighting-battles-wars-are-won-by-choosing/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points – General George S. Patton’s legendary success wasn’t

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: Building two stealthy sixth-generation fighters in
      parallel—F-47 and F/A-XX—would strain a U.S. industrial base that has consolidated
      into a handful of primes and a fragile supplier ecosystem. -Both programs demand
      elite engineering talent, secure software teams, advanced manufacturing, and high-end
      materials that are often single-source. -Workforce aging, clearance requirements,

      Problem That Generals and Admirals Can’t Patch Easily appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .'
    one_sentence_summary: The simultaneous development of two sixth-generation stealth
      fighters, the F-47 and F/A-XX, poses significant challenges for the U.S. military
      due to a consolidated industrial base, limited engineering talent, and reliance
      on single-source materials.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the challenges faced by the U.S. military
      in developing two sixth-generation stealth fighters, the F-47 and F/A-XX, simultaneously.
      It highlights the strain this dual development would place on an already consolidated
      industrial base, which relies on a limited number of prime contractors and a fragile
      supply chain. Key issues include the need for top-tier engineering talent, secure
      software teams, advanced manufacturing capabilities, and specialized materials
      that are often sourced from a single supplier. Additionally, factors such as an
      aging workforce, stringent clearance requirements, and increasing competition
      further complicate the situation, making it difficult for military leaders to
      address these challenges effectively.

    paragraph_summary: George S. Patton Jr., renowned for his speed, aggression, and
      victories in World War II, also faced significant setbacks, notably at Fort Driant

      battle. Death must not be feared." This quote reflects his belief in resilience
      and the importance of courage in the face of adversity.

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: The F-22 Raptor may still be America’s premier air-superiority

    one_sentence_summary: The F-22 Raptor remains the U.S. Air Force's top air-superiority

    paragraph_summary: The F-22 Raptor remains the U.S. Air Force's top air-superiority
      fighter, but maintaining its operational status has become increasingly costly
      due to the cessation of production, which limits economies of scale and complicates
      spare parts procurement. As a result, sustaining the small fleet of F-22s drives
      up the overall costs, with estimates suggesting that the per-jet price has escalated
      significantly. The article highlights the challenges faced by the Air Force in
      building new F-22 stealth fighters, emphasizing the financial and logistical hurdles
      involved in keeping the aging fleet functional.

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis became a formative

      while China struggled to track, target, or meaningfully contest them. -That discomfort
      helped drive a multi-decade modernization effort centered on persistent surveillance,
      long-range anti-ship strike, and an integrated reconnaissance-strike “kill chain.”

      Them appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis highlighted China's military
      vulnerabilities against U.S. aircraft carriers, prompting a long-term modernization
      effort focused on surveillance and strike capabilities to effectively counter
      them without necessarily sinking them.
    paragraph_summary: The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis highlighted China's military
      vulnerabilities, particularly its inability to effectively track and counter U.S.
      aircraft carriers operating near Taiwan. This experience prompted China to embark
      on a comprehensive modernization initiative focused on enhancing its surveillance
      capabilities, developing long-range anti-ship strike systems, and creating an
      integrated reconnaissance-strike "kill chain." As a result, China has evolved
      its military strategy, suggesting that it no longer needs to physically sink U.S.
      Navy aircraft carriers to neutralize their effectiveness in a potential conflict.

      capabilities, developing long-range anti-ship strike systems, and creating an

      adversaries like Russia and China.

      important assets, they would likely need to operate from greater distances, relying
      on long-range aircraft, refueling capabilities, standoff weapons, and reduced
      emissions to mitigate risks in such a scenario.

      sources instead of relying on public utilities, emphasizing energy-use transparency
      and prioritizing residential customers.
    paragraph_summary: A new bipartisan proposal, spearheaded by Missouri U.S. Senator
      Josh Hawley, aims to require large U.S. data centers that consume 20 megawatts
      or more to establish their own dedicated power generation instead of relying on
      public utilities. The legislation, known as the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from
      Data Centers Act, mandates energy-use disclosure from these facilities and emphasizes
      the need to prioritize residential customers during energy supply shortages.

      during the early Putin era.

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: As of February 13, 2026, the U.S. Air Force has officially
      denied reports that it received F-35 fighters with “empty radomes.” -Instead,

    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Air Force has denied claims of receiving F-35 fighters
      with "empty radomes," clarifying that the Lot 17 aircraft are equipped with older
      AN/APG-81 radar sets due to delays in the development of the advanced AN/APG-85
      radar.
    paragraph_summary: As of February 13, 2026, the U.S. Air Force has refuted claims
      that it received F-35 fighters with "empty radomes," clarifying that the Lot 17
      aircraft are being delivered with the older AN/APG-81 radar systems due to delays
      in the development of the next-generation AN/APG-85 radar. This situation highlights
      the reliance on two-decade-old technology while the new radar, which incorporates
      advanced Gallium technology, is still under development.

      during the submarine's assembly.

  - title: '$348,000,000,000 and Sinking: The U.S. Navy’s Columbia-class Submarine Fiasco'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/348000000000-and-sinking-the-u-s-navys-columbia-class-submarine-fiasco/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: America’s Ohio-class ballistic-missile submarines
      anchor the most survivable leg of the nuclear triad—yet Washington delayed their
      replacement and is now paying for it. -The Columbia-class program is colliding
      with shipyard manpower shortages, supplier delays, and the need to build Virginias
      at the same time, producing compressed schedules and rising costs. -A […] The
      post $348,000,000,000 and Sinking: The U.S. Navy’s Columbia-class Submarine Fiasco
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy's Columbia-class submarine program, essential
      for replacing the aging Ohio-class fleet, is facing significant delays and rising
      costs due to shipyard manpower shortages and simultaneous construction of other
      submarines.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the challenges facing the U.S. Navy's Columbia-class
      submarine program, which is intended to replace the aging Ohio-class ballistic-missile
      submarines that are crucial to the nuclear triad. Delays in the program's development
      have been exacerbated by shipyard manpower shortages, supplier delays, and the
      concurrent need to produce Virginia-class submarines, leading to compressed schedules
      and escalating costs. As a result, the Navy is facing significant financial and
      operational hurdles, with the Columbia-class program projected to cost $348 billion.
    published: '2026-02-13T18:08:32+00:00'

      faced a decline in support after the war, leading to only three being commissioned
      due to shifting military priorities.
    paragraph_summary: The Seawolf-class fast-attack submarine (SSN) is hailed as a
      remarkable achievement in Cold War naval engineering, characterized as the "quietest
      and deadliest" submarine designed for deep-sea operations. Constructed from HY-100
      steel for enhanced durability and capable of carrying 50 Tomahawk missiles, only
      three submarines of this class were commissioned due to a post-Cold War shift
      in military priorities towards more cost-effective alternatives. The article argues
      that the U.S. Navy's decision to limit the Seawolf program was a significant mistake,
      as it undermined the potential of this advanced submarine technology.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2026/02/undersea-gap-why-the-u-s-navy-cant-build-its-way-out-of-a-submarine-crisis/
    text: 'Summary and Key Points: As of February 2026, the U.S. Navy faces a critical
      “submarine squeeze” as aging attack boats retire faster than Virginia-class replacements
      arrive. -To bridge this gap, the Navy is shifting from experimental UUV research
      to operational deployment of Unmanned Undersea Systems as a combat-ready layer.
      -By offloading routine ISR, seabed monitoring, […] The post Undersea Gap: Why
      the U.S. Navy Can’t Build Its Way Out of a Submarine Crisis appeared first on
      19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: As of February 2026, the U.S. Navy is confronting a significant
      submarine shortage due to the rapid retirement of aging attack submarines, prompting
      a shift towards operational deployment of Unmanned Undersea Systems to compensate
      for the gap until Virginia-class replacements are fully operational.
    paragraph_summary: As of February 2026, the U.S. Navy is experiencing a significant
      "submarine squeeze," with older attack submarines being retired at a faster pace
      than new Virginia-class submarines can be deployed. To address this shortfall,
      the Navy is transitioning from experimental research on Unmanned Undersea Vehicles
      (UUVs) to their operational deployment as a combat-ready component, which will
      help alleviate some of the pressure by taking over routine tasks such as intelligence,
      surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR) and seabed monitoring. This strategy aims to
      mitigate the impact of the submarine crisis without solely relying on new construction.
    published: '2026-02-13T14:41:38+00:00'

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: The F-35 program has entered a high-stakes “radar
      gap” as Lot 17 aircraft are delivered to the U.S. military without their primary
      sensors. -Due to technical delays with the next-generation AN/APG-85 GaN radar
      and physical incompatibility with the older APG-81 mounts, these jets are currently
      flying with ballast plates to maintain […] The post Why the U.S. Air Force Is
      Delivering F-35 Stealth Fighters with “Weight Plates” Instead of Radars appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The F-35 program is facing significant challenges as Lot 17
      aircraft are being delivered to the U.S. military without their primary AN/APG-85
      radar systems, resulting in the use of ballast plates for weight balance due to
      technical delays and compatibility issues with older radar mounts.
    paragraph_summary: The F-35 program is facing significant challenges as it delivers
      Lot 17 aircraft to the U.S. military without their essential AN/APG-85 GaN radars,
      due to technical delays and compatibility issues with older APG-81 mounts. As
      a temporary measure, these jets are equipped with ballast plates to ensure proper
      weight distribution, highlighting a critical "radar gap" in the program's capabilities.

    text: 'Summary and Key Points: SR-71 pilot David Peters recently shared a legendary

    one_sentence_summary: SR-71 pilot David Peters recounted an extraordinary experience
